SCIENCE: Which observation shows that a seedling has grown?
its measured height increased over time
its pot has a new label
the room has a different poster
Two plants get the same soil and water but different amounts of light. What is being tested?
the effect of sunlight on growth
Why can tiny water drops appear outside a cold glass?
water vapor in nearby air condenses
the glass creates water from nothing
A puddle gets smaller on a sunny afternoon. What most likely happened?
some water evaporated into the air
Why does a sponge help clean up spilled water?
it absorbs some of the liquid
it pushes water into the air
Why does a tree's shadow often move during the day?
the sun's apparent position in the sky changes
the tree changes its roots each hour
What causes a plucked guitar string to make a sound?
Which object would an ordinary classroom magnet most likely attract?
Which tool is most useful for measuring a book's length?
Which tool tells us whether water is warmer or colder?
Which information should a weather chart record each day?
the name of the classroom pet
A frog begins as an egg, then becomes a tadpole. What happens next as it grows?
it develops legs and becomes a frog
Which is the best evidence that two objects have different masses?
one is closer to a window
Why do ducks have webbed feet?
webbing helps them push water when swimming
webbing makes them hatch from eggs
Why is it helpful to repeat an experiment?
to check whether the result happens again
If plants near a window lean toward the light, what could you investigate?
whether the direction of light affects growth
whether the room is painted yellow
When you see a rainbow, what is interacting with sunlight?
the dark side of the moon
Which change can be reversed by warming ice?
melting it back into liquid water
turning rust back into new iron
Which observation suggests a habitat has changed over a year?
fewer pond plants are counted each season
a student brings a new pen
one cloud has a different shape
A toy car rolls farther on a smooth floor than on thick carpet. What could explain this?
the two surfaces create different amounts of friction
A flashlight turns off when a wire is disconnected. Why?
the electrical circuit is no longer complete
Why do bicycle brakes help slow the wheels?
Which material usually transfers heat better?
What is a renewable source of energy?
When you let go of a dropped ball, which force pulls it toward Earth?
A river carries soil away from a bank. This is an example of…
A river drops sand when its water slows down. This process is called…
Why can bees help flowering plants reproduce?
they can carry pollen between flowers
Which animal undergoes a complete change from caterpillar to butterfly?
a characteristic passed from parents to offspring
a skill learned from a teacher
Which is mainly a physical change rather than making a new substance?
Sugar seems to disappear when stirred into water. What usually happened?
the sugar dissolved and spread through the water
What happens to a sound's pitch when its source vibrates faster?
Which container is best for measuring 100 milliliters of water?
Why do engineers build and test prototypes?
to discover what works and improve a design
to guarantee that a first idea is perfect
Why might introducing a new predator affect an ecosystem?
it can change how many prey animals survive
it makes every food chain identical
it stops all plants growing immediately
it removes the need for food
Which soil lets water drain through most quickly in a typical simple test?
What is a fair way to compare two paper-bridge designs?
use the same paper amount and loading method
test them with completely different weights
ignore the amount of paper used
Why should students record an unexpected result instead of hiding it?
it may help them improve their explanation
the notebook must always be full
it proves every original guess was wrong
Which action reduces waste before it is produced?
throwing away a new bottle each hour
A child compares two toy ramps using the same toy car. What must stay the same to compare ramp height fairly?
the starting push and the car
the color of the classroom walls
Two thermometers read 18°C and 23°C in different rooms. Which statement is supported by the measurements?
When comparing how fast ice melts in two bowls, which measurement gives useful evidence?
the time until each ice cube melts
the color of the bowls' labels
Students observe fewer birds at a feeder on rainy mornings. What is a careful next step?
collect counts over more days with similar observation times
decide rain always scares every bird
remove the dates from the observations
guess how many birds were there
Two seed groups receive different amounts of water and different amounts of light. Why is a conclusion about water alone difficult?
two conditions changed at the same time
A model bridge holds 8 kilograms in one test and 6 kilograms in another. What should students do before reporting its usual strength?
repeat fair trials and summarize all results
change the bridge design during each test
Two weather stations report different temperatures. Which detail should be checked before claiming a station is inaccurate?
whether the measurements were taken at the same time and location
how many photos were taken nearby
A class finds that a water filter removes visible soil but has not tested for microbes. Which claim is supported?
the water looks clearer but may still be unsafe to drink
the water is definitely safe to drink
all microbes are visible without magnification
the filter has removed every dissolved substance
GK: What does the legend on a map explain?
what its symbols and colors mean
A bar graph shows 9 apples and 6 pears. How many more apples are shown?
A library book is due on Friday. Today is Wednesday. How many days until it is due?
What is the safest place during a thunderstorm?
Why is a table useful when collecting daily temperatures?
it keeps observations organized for comparison
You have two quarters and one dime. How many cents is that?
Which source could help you find when a museum opens?
What is a scale on a map used for?
relating distances on a map to real distances
showing the weight of a book
counting the colors on a flag
Why should you read the title and labels on a graph?
to understand what the numbers represent
to avoid looking at the data
A map shows north at the top. Which direction is to your left?
If a 15-cent pencil and a 25-cent eraser are bought together, what is the total?
One bus leaves at 9:15 and another at 9:45. How much later is the second bus?
Which is strongest evidence that a town's buildings changed over time?
photographs of the same street from different years
a picture of an unrelated city
What does a primary source mean in a history investigation?
an original record or object from the time
Which online action best protects personal information?
asking a trusted adult before sharing private details
posting a home address in a public game
sending a password to a stranger
sharing a full name with unknown people
In a survey, 12 students choose swimming and 8 choose biking. How many were surveyed?
Why is it important to check when a news article was published?
the information may have changed since then
a random number with no reason
a number written only in words
Which method helps compare two products fairly?
check their price and the amount each contains
ignore the size of both products

THINKING_SEQUENCES: Plant a seed in soil, watch it sprout, and let it grow into a flowering plant.
Pack, check the route, travel and arrive at the destination.
Choose books, find facts, take notes and share what you learned.
Use soap and water, scrub your hands and dry them.
A chicken hatches from an egg, grows into a chick and then an adult.
Gather craft supplies, cut paper, fold it and make a card.
Rain leaves puddles, the weather clears, and plants can grow.
Get a basket, choose a food item, pay and take it home.
Take a photograph, study it, write a description and add it to a report.
Measure an object, record the numbers, graph them and discuss what they show.
Ask a testable question, test it, record results and decide what the evidence shows.
Heavy rain raises a river, flowing water moves sediment and rocks are exposed.
A pollinator visits a flower, pollen reaches another flower, seeds form and a new plant grows.
Collect preferences, tally them, make a graph and explain the results.
Mark a location, plan a route, navigate and arrive safely.
Choose a magnet, test a steel clip and a wooden object, then record what happened.
Sun warms water, water vapor forms clouds and rain falls.
Sketch a bridge, measure the materials, build it and test its strength.
Start a plant, photograph it, record observations by date and graph its growth.
Read a source, draft an explanation, check the evidence and revise your answer.
STORIES: Tomas designed a paper boat for the school pond. His first boat folded under the weight of a small pebble. He tried making the bottom wider and tested the new design using the same pebble. The second boat stayed afloat for longer. Tomas kept a record of both tests and planned to try another shape.
What did Tomas change in the second design?
the width of the boat's bottom
the weight of the pebble
the size of the pond
Why did he use the same pebble again?
to make the comparison fairer
to make the paper waterproof
to measure the pond's depth
What did Tomas learn from his tests?
changing a design can affect how it performs
all paper boats float for exactly the same time
pebbles always make boats move faster

The class wanted to know which plants attracted butterflies. Over three afternoons, they watched flowers in the garden and counted visiting butterflies. Yellow flowers had many visitors, but there were also more yellow flowers than other colors. Their teacher suggested counting visits per flower before deciding whether color mattered.
Why was counting only total butterfly visits misleading?
there were different numbers of flowers of each color
all butterflies avoid flowers
the class watched on three days
What did the teacher suggest?
compare visits per flower
remove all yellow flowers
guess which color is prettiest
What is the main lesson of the passage?
fair comparisons need the right measurements
a single count always proves a cause
flowers never attract insects

On Tuesday, Nadia borrowed a book about bridges. She learned that some bridges use arches and others use cables. On Wednesday she visited a footbridge with her uncle and took notes about its supports. She used the notes and book to make a labeled drawing for her class.
What two kinds of information did Nadia use?
a book and observations from a real bridge
two recipes
a weather chart and a calendar
Why did she label her drawing?
to show the important bridge parts
to make the paper heavier
to change the bridge's design
What did Nadia do after visiting the footbridge?
used her notes to make a drawing
built a car
forgot what she observed

The school cafeteria offered two lunches. One meal came with a reusable cup, and the other with a disposable bottle. Students counted the containers thrown away during a week. They presented the results to the principal and suggested using more reusable cups to reduce waste.
What did the students count?
discarded containers
the number of classrooms
the amount of sunlight
What was the goal of their suggestion?
reduce disposable waste
make lunches cost more
remove all drinks
Which detail supports their recommendation?
they collected a week of observations
they chose their favorite color
they read an unrelated story

Evan checked the library schedule before a visit. Story time began at ten o'clock, and the bus ride took twenty minutes. His family left at nine thirty so they would arrive before the program. They brought their library cards and returned two books on the way in.
How long before story time did Evan's family leave?
30 minutes
10 minutes
20 minutes
Why did they check the schedule?
to plan when to leave
to decide which books weighed more
to change the bus route
What did they do at the library?
returned books and attended story time
bought a bicycle
made a weather forecast

At a river cleanup, Maya noticed that plastic bottles collected near the park outnumbered cans. Her group recorded the types and locations of litter, then compared their findings with an older cleanup report. They learned that one day's results cannot reveal every long-term pattern. They proposed adding more bins and conducting another survey after several weeks. Their poster explained what they observed, what they inferred, and what they still did not know.
Why did Maya's group compare an older report?
to look for changes over time
to prove the park had no litter
to make the river flow faster
Which statement is an observation rather than an inference?
more plastic bottles than cans were collected near the park
the entire town will stop littering tomorrow
every bottle came from a visitor
Why did the group suggest another survey?
to gather more evidence
to avoid using the data
to make their poster longer

Owen built two model houses from cardboard. One had a wide roof, and the other had a steep roof. To compare how they handled rain, he poured the same amount of water onto each roof from the same height. Water ran off both, but the steep roof drained more quickly. Owen repeated the experiment and wrote that the slope seemed to affect drainage in his models. He did not claim that all real roofs would behave the same way.
What variable did Owen change?
the roof slope
the amount of water
the pouring height
What did the repeated tests suggest?
steeper roofs drained faster in his models
cardboard cannot get wet
all houses require the same roof
Why did Owen limit his conclusion?
a cardboard model cannot represent every real roof
water cannot be measured
he forgot which house he built

During a neighborhood walk, Leena used a map to compare two possible routes to a playground. The shorter route crossed a busy street, while the longer route used a marked crossing near a traffic light. She chose the longer route and explained that the safest option is not always the shortest. She recorded the distances so the family could plan future walks.
Why did Leena choose the longer route?
it used a safer crossing
she wanted to avoid the playground
the map showed no roads
What does the passage suggest about planning?
distance is only one consideration
shortest routes are always safest
maps cannot show streets
What information did she record?
route distances
the color of each car
the number of clouds

A class studied the way the moon appeared in the evening sky. Each student sketched the visible shape once a week. When they placed the sketches in date order, the class saw that the bright part changed. Their teacher explained that the moon reflects sunlight and that its appearance depends on the positions of Earth, the sun, and the moon. The students then predicted what a later sketch might show and checked their prediction.
What helped the students recognize a pattern?
placing the sketches in date order
drawing them with different pens
making every sketch the same
What causes the moon's changing appearance?
different views of its sunlit half
the moon turning off its own light
clouds permanently changing its shape
What did the students do after predicting?
made another observation to check
stopped watching the sky
changed the moon's orbit

The school garden committee was choosing between two watering systems. A sprinkler was quick to use, but some water landed on the sidewalk. A slow hose delivered water closer to the plants' roots. The students measured how much water each method used and considered the time needed. They recommended a method only after comparing the results and discussing tradeoffs.
What two factors did the committee compare?
water use and time
the colors of the hoses
the ages of the plants
Which is an example of a tradeoff in the passage?
a quick method may waste water
every method uses the same water
plants need no water
Why did the students measure both systems?
to support their choice with evidence
to guarantee no plants would ever wilt
to find the longest sidewalk

A team of students explored how different surfaces affected rolling toy cars. They made a wooden ramp and released the same car from the same marked height onto carpet, tile, and rough cardboard. On tile, the car rolled farthest. On carpet, it stopped sooner. They repeated each trial and calculated an average distance. Their report noted that friction might explain the difference, while also admitting that small measuring errors could affect their numbers.
Which variables did the students try to keep constant?
the car and the release height
the stopping distance
the type of surface
Why did they calculate an average?
to summarize repeated measurements
to make every trial identical
to avoid writing down results
What did they identify as a limitation?
possible measuring errors
the color of the ramp
the day of the week

A coastal town was deciding where to plant trees near a busy road. Children from two schools measured shade, recorded temperatures, and interviewed neighbors. The sites with more shade were cooler during several afternoon visits, but traffic and building shapes also varied. Their report recommended further observations and explained the difference between a pattern they saw and proof of a single cause. The town used the findings as one part of its planning process.
Why could the temperature pattern have more than one cause?
traffic and buildings also differed between sites
thermometers cannot measure outdoors
trees stop all traffic
Which statement is supported by the observations?
shadier sites were cooler during several visits
shade always reduces temperature by exactly ten degrees
all roads have identical temperatures
How did the town use the children's report?
as one source of evidence for planning
as proof that no more measurements were needed
to replace every road immediately

Students built a small rain garden using plants that could tolerate wet soil. Before planting, they tested how quickly water drained through different mixes of sand, soil, and compost. One mixture drained too rapidly for their chosen plants, and another stayed soggy. They selected a balanced mixture, planted the garden, and measured how it performed after several storms. The class wrote about both successful results and changes they would make next year.
What did the class test before planting?
how quickly water drained through soil mixtures
how high the school roof was
how quickly flowers changed color
Why did they avoid the fastest-draining mixture?
it did not suit the chosen plants' moisture needs
all sand is poisonous to plants
it made the garden too colorful
What made their investigation useful over time?
they monitored results after several storms
they ignored all unsuccessful tests
they measured only one flower once

At a local museum, Arjun examined photographs of a street taken in three different decades. An older picture showed small shops, while the most recent showed apartment buildings and a bicycle lane. He read newspaper reports to learn why some changes happened and interviewed a longtime resident for another perspective. In his report he separated details visible in the photographs from explanations that needed other sources. He also noted that one person's memory could be incomplete.
Which fact could Arjun verify directly from the photographs?
the street had a bicycle lane in the recent image
every resident supported the changes
all shops closed for the same reason
Why did he consult newspapers and an interview?
to investigate reasons not visible in photographs
to change the photographs
to avoid gathering evidence
What did he recognize about personal memories?
they can provide clues but may be incomplete
they always contain every detail
they replace all other historical sources

A robotics club tried to build a claw that could pick up a paper cup without crushing it. Their first model gripped too tightly, so they added a softer pad. The new design lifted the cup but occasionally dropped it. Students recorded how many times each version succeeded in ten trials. Instead of declaring victory after one good attempt, they compared results, adjusted the grip, and prepared a new test. They learned that improving an invention often means balancing competing needs.
What was the first design's problem?
it gripped too tightly
it could not be assembled
it had no movable parts
What evidence did the club collect?
the number of successful lifts in ten trials
the color of the cups alone
how much the students liked the pads
What tradeoff were they solving?
holding the cup firmly without crushing it
making every cup the same size
changing the cup into a different material

Mira's class weighed the paper they recycled each Friday. In the first week they collected 6 kilograms, in the second week 9 kilograms, and in the third week 7 kilograms. They made a bar chart and noticed the second week had the tallest bar. Their teacher reminded them that the chart described what they collected, not why the amount changed.
Which week had the most recycled paper?
the second week
the first week
the third week
How many kilograms were collected in the third week?
7 kilograms
9 kilograms
6 kilograms
Why did the teacher warn them about the chart?
it showed amounts but not the cause of changes
it proved the students stopped recycling
it could not show amounts at all

Elena planted two identical beans in separate pots. Both had the same soil, water, and sunny window. She added a small layer of mulch to one pot but not the other. Each morning she measured soil moisture at the same time. After five days, the mulched pot usually had moister soil. Elena wrote down the readings and planned to repeat the test.
What was different between the two pots?
one had a layer of mulch
one used a different bean
only one received water
Why did Elena measure at the same time?
to make the observations more comparable
to make the plant grow overnight
to keep the pots from moving
What can Elena reasonably report?
the mulched pot usually stayed moister in this test
mulch makes every plant grow twice as fast
water is unnecessary for bean plants

At the community garden, a path was too narrow for the wheelbarrow. Priya and Sam measured the wheelbarrow and the path with the same tape. The wheelbarrow was 58 centimeters wide, and the path was 54 centimeters wide. They suggested widening the path to 70 centimeters and drew a plan before asking a grown-up to help.
What made the path difficult to use?
it was narrower than the wheelbarrow
it was too long to measure
it had too many flowers
How much wider was the wheelbarrow than the path?
4 centimeters
12 centimeters
16 centimeters
Why did they draw a plan first?
to explain the proposed change before building
to make the wheelbarrow heavier
to avoid measuring the path

On a windy day, Noor tested a kite in the school field. Her first flight lasted eight seconds before the kite dipped. She shortened the tail but kept the same kite and string. Her next flight lasted twelve seconds. Noor knew that a change in wind could also affect a flight, so she planned several more trials before making a conclusion.
What did Noor change for the second flight?
the length of the kite's tail
the size of the school field
the type of kite
How long did the second flight last?
twelve seconds
eight seconds
twenty seconds
Why did Noor want more trials?
wind changes could also affect flight time
one test can never be recorded
every kite must fly the same way

Students measured how much water three garden beds needed during one warm week. The raised bed used 12 liters, the shaded bed used 8 liters, and the bed near the wall used 10 liters. But the raised bed also had more plants than the others. Their teacher asked them to calculate water use per plant before deciding which location was most efficient. The class agreed that an amount alone does not always make a fair comparison.
Which bed used the least total water?
the shaded bed
the raised bed
the bed near the wall
Why might total water use be a misleading comparison?
the beds did not contain the same number of plants
the water was measured in liters
all the beds were in the same garden
What would make the comparison fairer?
calculate water used per plant
ignore how many plants grew there
assume the raised bed wasted water

Two routes connect the school and the pool. Route A is 1.8 kilometers long and crosses one busy intersection. Route B is 2.1 kilometers long but has a protected crossing. The class compared distance and safety rather than choosing by distance alone. They invited a crossing guard to explain how traffic changes during the afternoon. The students recommended the protected route for their walking group, even though it was longer.
Which route was shorter?
Route A
Route B
both routes were equal
Why did the students consider the crossing guard's advice?
the shortest route was not necessarily the safest
the guard could shorten the road
traffic never changes during the day
What tradeoff did they choose?
a longer route with a protected crossing
the least walking with no crossings
a faster route regardless of traffic

A science club tested the temperature of a sunny paved courtyard and a shaded grassy corner. At noon, the pavement read 34°C and the shaded grass read 27°C. The club wanted to know whether shade or surface material explained the difference. Their first test changed both factors at once. They designed another test using two similar paved areas, one shaded and one sunny, so only the amount of shade would differ.
How much warmer was the sunny pavement than the shaded grass?
Why could the first comparison not isolate the effect of shade?
both shade and surface material were different
the thermometers displayed Celsius
the readings were taken at noon
What improvement did the club make?
compare similar paved surfaces with different shade
measure only the sunny spot again
replace the thermometer with a ruler

After heavy rain, a stream near the school looked muddy. Students wondered if soil was washing from a nearby bare slope. They collected water samples upstream and downstream of the slope on the same afternoon, using identical clear containers. Downstream water contained more visible sediment. The students recorded that the samples supported their idea, but they avoided claiming the slope was the only possible cause.
Where did students find more visible sediment?
downstream of the bare slope
in every sample equally
only in the empty containers
Why did they use identical containers?
to make the water samples easier to compare
to change the direction of the stream
to remove the soil from the slope
What was a reasonable conclusion?
the evidence supported a possible source, not the only cause
the bare slope was proved to be the only cause
rain cannot change water clarity

The town museum planned a new exhibit about local transportation. One visitor asked for larger print labels, while another wanted a model that could be touched. The team interviewed visitors and tested prototypes with several groups. A large-print label helped many readers, but the raised model also needed clear spoken guidance. The final exhibit included multiple ways to explore the same information, because no single format worked for everyone.
What did visitors ask the museum to improve?
how people could access exhibit information
the museum's opening year
the color of the parking lot
Why did the team test more than one prototype?
different visitors needed different ways to learn
every visitor gave exactly the same feedback
one format always suits everyone
What can be inferred about the team's goal?
make the exhibit usable by more visitors
replace every object with a sign
remove visitor feedback from decisions

To learn how children travelled to school, a class surveyed only the students who arrived on the first bus. Of the twenty students surveyed, sixteen said they used a bus. Maya noted that the sample excluded children who walked or cycled in later. The class changed its plan and asked students from several arrival groups. Their new survey gave a more balanced picture of the ways classmates reached school.
Why was the first survey biased?
it mostly sampled children from one bus
it asked students how they travelled
it counted exactly twenty answers
What did the class change?
they surveyed several different arrival groups
they removed walking from the choices
they asked only the bus driver
What is the main lesson?
who you survey can affect the result
a larger number always proves a claim
all students travel the same way

A class built paper seed models to explore how wind might carry real seeds. They made four copies of each design and dropped them from the same height in the gym. A fan blew at one speed for every trial. One design travelled farther on average, but its results varied. The class compared all trials rather than picking the longest flight and suggested testing outdoors next, where wind changes more often.
Which condition did the class keep the same?
the fan speed during each trial
the shape of every seed model
the distance travelled by every model
Why did they compare all trials?
a single longest flight may not be typical
the longest flight always proves a design is best
only failed flights are useful
What limitation did the class recognize?
real outdoor wind can vary more than their gym test
paper models are living seeds
the fan made measurement impossible

Leo studied weather records from his town. A diary from a hundred years ago described one unusually snowy winter. Recent records covered thirty complete winters, including several mild ones and several snowy ones. Leo's friend wanted to compare that single old winter with the thirty-year average. Leo explained that an unusual year can happen even when long-term patterns differ, and suggested finding more historical years before drawing a conclusion.
What made the older diary less useful for comparing long-term patterns?
it described only one winter
it was written by hand
it mentioned snow
What did Leo suggest collecting?
records from more historical winters
only the coldest day last year
photographs of summer flowers
Which conclusion fits the evidence best?
one unusual winter does not establish a long-term pattern
all winters used to be snowier
weather never varies between years
